title: Data & Averages
description: Collecting, displaying and interpreting data using bar charts, pictograms and pie charts. Finding the mean, median, mode and range.

notes.heading: Collecting and Organising Data
notes.body: Data is collected through surveys, measurements, or experiments. Organise into frequency tables (value + count). Use tally marks (groups of 5: four lines + diagonal). For many values, group into class intervals (0−9, 10−19, etc.). Always label tables clearly.

notes.heading: Bar Charts, Pictograms and Pie Charts
notes.body: Bar chart: bar height = frequency, equal bar widths, equal gaps, labelled axes. Pictogram: pictures represent values — always check the key (e.g., one star = 5 books). Pie chart: shows parts of a whole — each sector angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.

notes.heading: Mean, Median, Mode and Range
notes.body: Mean = sum ÷ count. Median = middle value when ordered (average two middle values if even count). Mode = most frequent value. Range = max − min. Example: 3,5,7,4,6 → mean=5, median=5, no single mode, range=4.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Average
notes.body: Mean: uses every value, affected by outliers. Median: better with outliers (e.g., 2,3,4,4,100 → mean=22.6, median=4). Mode: best for non-numerical data or most common answer. Always report an average + range for a complete picture.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Mean vs median confusion
notes.body: The mean uses every value, so one very large or small value can pull it up or down. The median only cares about the middle value, so it is more reliable when data has extreme values. Always decide which average tells the story best.

notes.heading: ✅ Reading scales on charts
notes.body: Before reading a bar chart, check what each small square or grid line represents. If one square stands for 2 students, a bar halfway between 10 and 12 represents 11 students, not 10.5 unless the scale says so.

questions.explanation: Range = maximum value − minimum value. The maximum is 19 and the minimum is 3, so 19 − 3 = 16.

questions.stem: Scores: 8,7,9,6,10. Next test score is 2. Which average is most affected?
questions.explanation: Mean drops significantly with the outlier of 2.

questions.stem: Data: dogs=8, cats=5, fish=3, rabbits=4. Best chart for proportions?
questions.explanation: Pie chart best shows parts of a whole.

questions.stem: Survey of 30: 15 blue, 9 red, 6 green. Pie chart angle for blue?
Mean=8, median=6, mode=5. What's likely true?
questions.explanation: Mean > median suggests outliers pulling the mean higher.

questions.stem: Five students' quiz scores are 7, 9, 6, 8, and 10. What is their mean score?
The median of a set of numbers is 8. If you add the number 50 to the set, will the median always stay at 8?
choices: No, it depends on the size of the set and the order
questions.explanation: For an odd number of values, the median may stay the same if 50 is placed at one end. For an even number, adding one value changes the middle. So it depends on the original data.

questions.stem: The mean of four test scores is 72. After a fifth test, the mean rises to 76. What was the fifth test score?
questions.explanation: Total of first four = 4 × 72 = 288. Total of five = 5 × 76 = 380. Fifth score = 380 − 288 = 92.
